title: Anomalous transport in periodic systems driven by active fluctuations
abstract: This dissertation investigates the transport of Brownian particles driven by active fluctuations in periodic potential landscapes. Unlike thermal noise, active fluctuations break detailed balance and violate the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. They model self-propulsion mechanisms and active-bath interactions in biological and synthetic micro-systems. By focusing on white Poisson shot noise with non-Gaussian amplitude statistics, this work systematically uncovers the mechanisms governing three major transport anomalies: giant transport enhancement, absolute negative mobility, and the ratchet effect.   Combining Monte Carlo simulations with analytical modeling, this work demonstrates that active fluctuations adhering to a bidirectional skew-normal amplitude distribution enhance directed velocity compared to the free-particle by several orders of magnitude. This giant transport enhancement is fully quantified via a phenomenological jump-relaxation model that decouples particle displacement into instantaneous stochastic jumps and deterministic relaxation towards potential minimum. Extending this model to inertial dynamics reveals that finite particle mass m acts as a dynamic control parameter capable of strengthening, weakening, constructively inducing, or completely suppressing transport enhancement depending on noise variance.   Furthermore, an ultra-minimal model for absolute negative mobility is established in a one-dimensional, purely overdamped system, showing that discontinuous shot noise drives transport opposite to an applied bias without requiring particle inertia, nonlinearity of spatially periodic potential, or explicit time-dependent periodic driving. Conversely, under an alternative scaling of the average stochastic force, an asymmetric distribution of fluctuation amplitudes generates net directed transport through a tilting ratchet effect in the zero-bias limit.
summary: This research explores how active, non-thermal fluctuations drive anomalous transport in periodic systems, leading to phenomena like giant enhancement and negative mobility. By modeling the noise statistically, the authors quantify these effects using jump-relaxation models. The findings offer theoretical insights into energy transduction in synthetic and biological active matter systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the non-equilibrium transport of Brownian particles driven by active fluctuations within periodic potential landscapes.
main_result: Active fluctuations can induce giant transport enhancement, absolute negative mobility, and directed motion (ratchet effect) through mechanisms that violate detailed balance.
method: The work combines high-precision Monte Carlo simulations with analytical modeling, developing phenomenological jump-relaxation models.
model_or_system: The system models Brownian particles in periodic potentials, driven by active fluctuations characterized by white Poisson shot noise with non-Gaussian amplitude statistics. This contrasts with standard thermal noise.
key_observables: Giant directed velocity enhancement, absolute negative mobility, and the magnitude of directed current in the zero-bias limit.
important_parameters: Noise variance, particle mass (m), and the statistics of the fluctuation amplitudes (e.g., bidirectional skew-normal distribution).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling active noise as white Poisson shot noise and employing a jump-relaxation framework to decouple particle dynamics.
figures_summary: Not specified (Notes suggest quantitative demonstration of enhancement and negative mobility via modeling).
paper_structure: The dissertation systematically covers the theoretical distinction between thermal and active fluctuations, dedicating sections to the mechanisms and quantification of giant transport enhancement, absolute negative mobility, and the ratchet effect.
why_interesting: The study provides concrete, non-equilibrium examples of directed transport and energy dissipation far from equilibrium, which are crucial concepts in understanding open quantum systems and energy flow in mesoscopic physics.
